en.content: A mass M is suspended by a rope from a rigid support at A as shown in figure. Another rope is tied at the end B, and it is pulled horizontally with a force F. If the rope AB makes an angle $\theta$ with the vertical in equilibrium, then the tension in the string AB is :
en.explanation:
At point B horizontal force ($F$) is horizontally to the right.

Downward tension ($T_{\text{lower}}$) which supports the block of mass M.

In equilibrium, the tension in this vertical rope balances the weight of the mass.

$$T_{\text{lower}} = Mg$$

acting vertically downwards.

Tension in segment AB ($T_{AB}$) is along the rope from B towards A making an angle $\theta$ with the vertical line.

The vertical component of tension points upwards:

$$T_y = T_{AB} \cos \theta$$

The horizontal component of tension points to the left

$$T_x = T_{AB} \sin \theta$$

Since the system is in perfect static equilibrium, the net force in both the horizontal and vertical directions must equal zero.

$$\Sigma F_x = 0$$

$$T_{AB} \sin \theta = F$$

$$T_{AB} = \frac{F}{\sin \theta}$$

Therefore, the correct option is (B).

en.content: Two persons are holding a light rope tightly at its ends so that it is horizontal. A 15 kg weight is attached to the rope at the midpoint which now no longer remains horizontal. The minimum tension required to completely straighten the rope is :
en.explanation:
Let the tension in both segments of the light rope be T (due to symmetry). Let $\theta$ be the angle that the rope makes with the true horizontal line at the points of support.

The downward gravitational force acting on the mass is $\mathrm{W}=\mathrm{mg}=15 \mathrm{~g}$, where g is the acceleration due to gravity.

Each half of the rope pulls upwards with a tension force T at an angle $\theta$ above the horizontal.

On resolving the forces vertically for the midpoint mass in equilibrium

$$\sum F_y = 0$$

$$T \sin \theta + T \sin \theta = mg$$

$$2T \sin \theta = 15g$$

$$T = \frac{15g}{2\sin \theta}$$

T in kg-force $= \frac{15}{2\sin \theta}$

For the rope to become horizontal angle must be zero.

$$\theta \rightarrow 0^\circ \Rightarrow \sin(0^\circ) = 0$$

$$T = \frac{15}{2 \times 0} \rightarrow \infty$$

Therefore, the correct option is (D).

en.content: A sphere of mass $m$ is kept between two inclined walls, as shown in the figure. If the coefficient of friction between each wall and the sphere is zero then the ratio of normal reaction $\left(\frac{N_1}{N_2}\right)$ offered by the walls 1 and 2 on the sphere will be
en.explanation:
Wall 1 forms an angle $\theta$ with respect to this horizontal baseline.

Wall 2 forms an angle $\theta$ with respect to Wall 1 .

Therefore, the total inclination angle that Wall 2 makes with the horizontal is equal to $\theta+\theta=2 \theta$.

Since the contact surfaces are smooth, the contact forces (normal reactions) act perpendicular to the respective walls and pass directly through the centre of the sphere.

For Wall 1 , which is inclined at an angle $\theta$ to the horizontal, its normal reaction force $\mathrm{N}_1$ acts perpendicular to it, making an angle $\theta$ with the vertical line.

The horizontal component of this force is $\mathrm{N}_{1 \mathrm{x}}=\mathrm{N}_1 \sin \theta$

The vertical component is $\mathrm{N}_{1 \mathrm{y}}=\mathrm{N}_1 \cos \theta$.

For Wall 2, which is inclined at an angle $2 \theta$ to the horizontal, its normal reaction force $\mathrm{N}_2$ acts perpendicular to it, making an angle $2 \theta$ with the vertical line.

The horizontal component of this force is $N_{2x} = N_2 \sin(2\theta)$

The vertical component is $N_{2y} = N_2 \cos(2\theta)$

Since the sphere remains at rest, it is in complete static equilibrium. Therefore, the net horizontal force acting on the sphere must equal zero:

$$\sum F_x = 0$$

$$N_2 \sin(2\theta) - N_1 \sin \theta = 0$$

$$N_1 \sin \theta = N_2 \sin(2\theta)$$

$$\frac{N_1}{N_2} = \frac{\sin(2\theta)}{\sin \theta}$$

Using trigonometric double angle formula $\sin(2\theta) = 2 \sin \theta \cos \theta$

$$\frac{N_1}{N_2} = \frac{2 \sin \theta \cos \theta}{\sin \theta}$$

$$\frac{N_1}{N_2} = 2 \cos \theta$$

Therefore, the correct option is (C).

en.content:
A string is wrapped round a log of wood and it is pulled with a force F as shown in the figure. Choose the correct statement(s).


I. Tension T in the string decreases with increase in θ

II. Tension T > F if $\theta > \frac{\pi}{3}$
en.explanation:
The pulling force F is applied symmetrical about central line.

Let the tension force in string is T and the angle that each of these string segments makes with the line of action of the pulling force F is $\theta$.

On resolving the tension forces into components parallel and perpendicular to the force F :

The components perpendicular to the line of action of F are $T\sin\theta$ acting in opposite directions.

These two perpendicular components cancel each other

$$\sum F_y = T\sin\theta - T\sin\theta = 0$$

The components parallel to the line of action of F both act in the direction opposite to F.

The magnitude of tension parallel to the line of action from each segment equal to $T\cos\theta$.

For the system to be in a state of static equilibrium, the sum of all forces along the line of action of F must equal zero:

$$\sum F_x = 0$$

$$F - T\cos\theta - T\cos\theta = 0$$

$$F = 2T\cos\theta$$

$$T = \frac{F}{2\cos\theta}$$

In the first quadrant as $\theta$ increases from $0^\circ$ toward $90^\circ$, the value of $\cos\theta$ decreases.

Because $\cos\theta$ is in the denominator of formula $T = \frac{F}{2\cos\theta}$, a decrease in the denominator causes the total value of the fraction to increase. Therefore, the tension $T$ must increase as $\theta$ increases. So, statement I is false.

$$\frac{F}{2\cos\theta} > F$$

$$\frac{1}{2\cos\theta} > 1$$

$$1 > 2\cos\theta$$

$$\cos\theta < \frac{1}{2}$$

As cosine function decreases as the angle increases in this range, the condition

$$\cos\theta < \frac{1}{2} \Rightarrow \theta > \frac{\pi}{3}$$

Therefore, Statement II is true.

Since Statement I is false and Statement II is true, the correct option is (C).

en.content: AB is a string whose one end A is fixed at the highest point of a ring placed in vertical plane. C is the centre of the ring. At other end B of the string, is attached a bead of mass m, which can slide along the ring. If the bead is in equilibrium at B and string is taut then the tension in the string is :
en.explanation:
Point A is fixed at the highest point of a vertical ring, and C is the centre of that ring, so the line segment AC is a vertical radius of the ring.

The segment BC is another radius connecting the centre to the position of the bead B . The string is represented by the chord AB .

Let R be the radius of the ring, $\mathrm{AC}=\mathrm{BC}=\mathrm{R}$.

Because $AC = BC$, triangle ABC is an isosceles triangle. In any isosceles triangle, the angles opposite the equal sides must be equal.

The angle at vertex B between the chord AB and the radius BC is $\angle ABC = \theta$. Therefore, the angle at vertex A must also be equal to $\angle BAC = \theta$.

Since the sum of all interior angles in any triangle is always $180^{\circ}$, the angle at the centre is,

$$\angle ACB = 180^{\circ} - (\angle ABC + \angle BAC)$$

$$\angle ACB = 180^{\circ} - (\theta + \theta) = 180^{\circ} - 2\theta$$

The forces acting on the bead of mass m at point B:

The force of gravity $(mg)$ acts vertically downward.

Tension $(T)$ acts along the taut string, directed from point B toward point A.

Normal reaction $(N)$ acts perpendicular to the surface of the smooth ring, which is along the radial line CB.

Since the bead is free to slide along the smooth ring without friction, it can only be in static equilibrium if the net force acting along the tangential direction of the ring is zero.

The angle between the vertical line CA and the radial line CB is $\angle ACB = 180^{\circ} - 2\theta$.

So, the angle between the downward vertical line and the radial line CB is the supplementary angle

$$\alpha = 180^{\circ} - (180^{\circ} - 2\theta) = 2\theta$$

Therefore, the component of gravity acting along the tangent line is $mg \sin \alpha = mg \sin(2\theta)$.

Equating the tangential components for equilibrium:

$$T \sin \theta = mg \sin(2\theta)$$

Using trigonometric identity, $\sin(2\theta) = 2 \sin \theta \cos \theta$

$$T \sin \theta = mg(2 \sin \theta \cos \theta)$$

$$T = 2mg \cos \theta$$

Therefore, the tension in string is $2mg \cos \theta$. Thus, the correct option is (C).

en.content:
Two smooth cylindrical bars weighing $W$ N each lie next to each other in contact. A similar third bar is placed over the two bars as shown in figure.

Neglecting friction, the minimum horizontal force on each lower bar necessary to keep them together is :
en.explanation:
Let R is the radius of each cylinder.

When two identical cylinders are in contact with one another, the straight-line distance between their centres is equal to the sum of their radii, which is $R+R=2 R$.

Because each of the three cylinders touches the other two, the lines connecting their three centres form a triangle where every side has an equal length of 2 R .

A triangle with three equal sides is an equilateral triangle, and all of its interior angles are $60^{\circ}$.

The normal reaction force N between any two smooth cylinders in contact must act along the line connecting their centres.

The angle that the line of centres makes with the vertical line is $\alpha=90^{\circ}-60^{\circ}=30^{\circ}$.

By symmetry the normal contact force between top cylinder and either of cylinders on ground must be equal.

$$ \mathrm{N}_{\mathrm{AC}}=\mathrm{N}_{\mathrm{AB}}=\mathrm{N} $$

For the cylinder A (top cylinder)

For the top cylinder to remain at rest, the net vertical force must equal zero :

$$\Sigma F_y = 0$$

$$N_{AC} \cos(30^\circ) + N_{AB} \cos(30^\circ) - W = 0$$

$$2N \cos(30^\circ) = W$$

$$2N\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) = W \Rightarrow N = \frac{W}{\sqrt{3}}$$

For cylinder B.

The forces acting on it are its weight $W$ downward, the upward normal force from the ground, the normal reaction $N_{BA} = N$ from the top cylinder, and the horizontal pushing force $F$ to the right.

For this lower cylinder to remain in horizontal equilibrium, the net horizontal force must equal zero:

$$\Sigma F_x = 0$$

$$F - N\sin\alpha - N_{BC} = 0$$

$$F - N\sin(30^\circ) - N_{BC} = 0$$

$$F = N\sin(30^\circ) + N_{BC}$$

For minimum value of force $F$, we assume the two cylinders $B$ and $C$ on horizontal ground are just touching each other, i.e., the normal contact force between them is zero, $N_{BC} = N_{CB} = 0$

$$F = (W\sqrt{3}) \times \frac{1}{2}$$

$$F = \frac{W}{2/\sqrt{3}}$$

Therefore, the correct option is (D).

en.content: Two blocks of mass 6 kg and 4 kg are pushed along a horizontal frictionless surface by a force of 40 N applied to the 6 kg block at an angle of $60^\circ$ to the horizontal. The force that the 4 kg block exerts on the 6 kg block is :
en.explanation:
The mass of the first block is $\mathrm{m}_1=6 \mathrm{~kg}$, and the mass of the second block is $\mathrm{m}_2=4 \mathrm{~kg}$.

The external force applied to the first block is $\mathrm{F}=40 \mathrm{~N}$ at an angle of $\theta=60^{\circ}$ relative to the horizontal surface.

Since the blocks are resting on a rigid horizontal floor, they cannot move vertically. The vertical component of the applied force pushes down into the ground and is balanced by the normal reaction force from the floor.

Therefore, only the horizontal component of the applied force causes the blocks to accelerate along the frictionless surface.

The horizontal component of the applied force is

$$ \mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{x}}=\mathrm{F} \cos \left(60^{\circ}\right)=\frac{\mathrm{F}}{2}=\frac{40 \mathrm{~N}}{2}=20 \mathrm{~N} $$

This net horizontal force acts toward the right, pushing the entire block system forward.

The total mass of system is

$$ \mathrm{M}=\mathrm{m}_1+\mathrm{m}_2=6 \mathrm{~kg}+4 \mathrm{~kg}=10 \mathrm{~kg} $$

Applying Newton's second law to the combined system the common acceleration a of the system is,

$$ \begin{gathered} \mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{x}}=\mathrm{M} \cdot \mathrm{a} \\ 20=10 \cdot \mathrm{a} \\ \mathrm{a}=\frac{20}{10}=2 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2 \end{gathered} $$

The positive sign shows that the system is accelerating towards right.

Let $\mathrm{N}_{\mathrm{c}}$ be the magnitude of the normal force that the blocks exert on each other.

For the 4 kg block $\left(\mathrm{m}_2\right)$ the only horizontal force acting on this block is the pushing force exerted on it by the 6 kg block, which acts toward the right.

Applying Newton's second law to block $m_2$:

$$\Sigma F_x = m_2 \cdot a$$

$$N_c = 4 \times 2\,\mathrm{N} = 8\,\mathrm{N}$$

This means the $6\,\mathrm{kg}$ block pushes the $4\,\mathrm{kg}$ block to the right with a force of $8\,\mathrm{N}$.

According to Newton's third law of motion, every action has an equal and opposite reaction. Therefore, if the $6\,\mathrm{kg}$ block exerts an $8\,\mathrm{N}$ force on the $4\,\mathrm{kg}$ block to the right, the $4\,\mathrm{kg}$ block must simultaneously exert a force of equal magnitude ($8\,\mathrm{N}$) on the $6\,\mathrm{kg}$ block directed in the opposite direction, which is to the left.

Therefore, the correct option is (A).

en.content: Two trucks pull on either end of a rope, each with a force of 10,000 N. In the centre of the rope, a ball of mass 20 kg is hanging. The angle $\theta$ that the rope makes with the horizontal is :

options.content: $0^{\circ}$, the rope will obviously be horizontal in this situation

en.explanation:
The system is symmetrical because the ball hangs in the centre and both trucks pull with the same force magnitude.

Therefore, the tension $T$ in both segments of the rope is equal to the pulling force of the trucks:

$$T = 10{,}000 {N}$$

The mass of the hanging ball is $m = 20 { kg}$.

The downward gravitational force (weight) acting on the ball is:

$$W = m . g$$

$$W = 20 \times 10 = 200{ N}$$

Each side of the rope is inclined at an angle $\theta$ with respect to the horizontal baseline.

Along horizontal direction the left segment pulls to the left with a component of $T\cos\theta$ and the right segment pulls to the right with a component of $T\cos\theta$.

These two equal and opposite forces cancel each other.

$$\Sigma F_x = T\cos\theta - T\cos\theta = 0$$

So, the system is in horizontal equilibrium.

Along vertical direction, for the equilibrium of system;

$$\Sigma F_y = 0$$

$$T\sin\theta + T\sin\theta - m\cdot g = 0$$

$$2T\sin\theta = m\cdot g$$

$$\sin\theta = \frac{mg}{2T}$$

$$\sin\theta = \frac{200}{2 \times 10{,}000}$$

$$\sin\theta = 0.01$$

Since the value of $\sin\theta$ is very small, the angle $\theta$ will also be very small.

For small angles measured in radians, using small-angle approximation where $\sin\theta \approx \theta$.

Therefore:

$$\theta \approx 0.01\text{ radians} = 0.01 \times \frac{180^\circ}{\pi}$$

$$\theta \approx 0.56^\circ$$

Therefore, the correct option is (C).

en.content: A smooth cylinder of mass M and radius R is resting on two corner edges A and B as shown in figure. The normal reaction at the edges A and B are :
en.explanation:
The normal reaction forces must act perpendicular to the tangent of the cylinder's surface at points of contact. For any circle or cylinder, a line that is perpendicular to the surface at any point always passes directly through its centre. Therefore, the normal reaction force from corner $\mathrm{A}\left(\mathrm{N}_{\mathrm{A}}\right)$ and the normal reaction force from corner B $\left(N_B\right)$ are both along the radii straight toward the centre of the cylinder.

The normal force $N_A$ is making an angle of $\alpha = 60^{\circ}$ with the vertical.

The normal force $N_B$ is making an angle of $\beta = 30^{\circ}$ with the vertical.

Since the cylinder is at rest, the sum of all horizontal forces acting on the cylinder must equal zero.

$$\Sigma F_x = 0$$

$$N_A \sin(60^{\circ}) - N_B \sin(30^{\circ}) = 0 \Rightarrow N_A\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) = N_B\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)$$

$$\Rightarrow N_A\sqrt{3} = N_B$$

$$\Rightarrow N_B = \sqrt{3}N_A$$

Therefore, the correct option is (D).

en.content: A bird sits on a light wire stretched horizontally between two points. The tension in the wire now is :

options.content: equal to the weight of the bird
greater than the weight of the bird
less than the weight of the bird

en.explanation:
The wire is initially stretched horizontally between two rigid supports.

A bird of mass $m$ lands on the wire, which introduces a downward vertical force equal to the bird's weight :

$$ \mathrm{W}=\mathrm{mg} $$

When the bird sits on the wire, the wire cannot remain horizontal. If it stayed horizontal, the tension forces inside the wire would act horizontally and would have no vertical component to balance the downward force of gravity, making static equilibrium impossible.

Therefore, the wire must deform downward by some small angle $\theta$ relative to the horizontal.

The wire is divided into two segments, each pulling away from the bird with a tension force $T$.

Horizontal components of the two segments pull in opposite directions with a magnitude of $T\cos\theta$, canceling each other out.

Vertical components at both the tensions equal to $T\sin\theta$.

For the bird to remain in vertical static equilibrium, the sum of the vertical components must balance the downward weight of the bird:

$$\Sigma F_y = 0 \Rightarrow T\sin\theta + T\sin\theta = mg$$

$$2T\sin\theta = mg$$

$$T = \frac{mg}{2\sin\theta}$$

Because the wire is tightly stretched between two fixed points, it only sags by a very small amount, so the angle $\theta$ is quite small (let less than $30^\circ$).

$$\sin\theta < 0.5$$

$$2\sin\theta < 2 \times 0.5 \Rightarrow 2\sin\theta < 1$$

$$T = \frac{mg}{2\sin\theta} > mg$$

Therefore, the tension developed in the wire is greater than the weight of the bird. Thus the correct option is (C).

The mass of the block is $\mathrm{M}=10 \mathrm{~kg}$, and the inclination angle is $\theta=30^{\circ}$.

The component of this weight acting down along the slope is $\mathrm{Mg} \sin \left(30^{\circ}\right)$.

The light, inextensible string connects block M to the hanging mass m passing over an ideal pulley at the top.

This tension force T pulls block M up along the slope.

For block M to remain in static equilibrium, the net force parallel to the incline must be zero:

$$\Sigma F_{\parallel} = 0$$

$$T - Mg\sin(30^{\circ}) = 0$$

$$T = Mg\sin(30^{\circ}) \ldots (i)$$

For the hanging mass m the upward tension force T from the string and the downward force of gravity equal to its weight, $mg$.

For mass m to remain at rest, the net vertical force must be zero:

$$\Sigma F_y = 0$$

$$T - mg = 0 \rightarrow T = mg \ldots (ii)$$

From both the equations,

$$mg = Mg\sin(30^{\circ})$$

$$m = M\sin(30^{\circ})$$

Substituting the given mass $M = 10\ \mathrm{kg}$,

$$m = 10 \times \sin(30^{\circ})$$

$$m = 10 \times \frac{1}{2}\ \mathrm{kg} = 5\ \mathrm{kg}$$

Therefore, the value of $m$ is $5\ \mathrm{kg}$ so that $M = 10\ \mathrm{kg}$ remains in equilibrium.

attached to block.

en.content: A flexible chain of weight $W=15 N$ hangs between two fixed points $A$ and $B$ at the same level. The inclination of the chain with the horizontal at the two points of support is $\theta$. If the tension of the chain at the endpoint is $x$$$\cos ec\theta $$ then find value of $10x$.
en.explanation:
The chain is supported symmetrically at its two endpoints, A and B, which lie on the same horizontal level.

Gravitational force ( W ) acts vertically downwards from the centre of mass of the chain.

Tension at support $\mathrm{A}(\mathrm{T})$ pulls along the tangent of the chain at point A at an angle $\theta$ relative to the horizontal line.

Tension at support $\mathrm{B}(\mathrm{T})$ due to the symmetry, the tension magnitude at point B is also T , directed upwards at the same angle $\theta$ relative to the horizontal line.

At support point A horizontal component of tension in string is $\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{x}}=\mathrm{T} \cos \theta$ and the vertical component is $\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{y}}=\mathrm{T} \sin \theta$.

At support point B horizontal component of tension in string is $\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{x}}=\mathrm{T} \cos \theta$ and the vertical component is $\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{y}}=\mathrm{T} \sin \theta$.

The horizontal components at A and B are equal in magnitude and in opposite directions

$$ \mathrm{T} \cos \mathrm{v}-\mathrm{T} \cos \theta=0 $$

So, the chain is in equilibrium along horizontal.

The combined upward vertical pulling forces from both supports must balance the total downward weight W of the flexible chain for equilibrium along vertical direction.

$$ \mathrm{T} \sin \theta+\mathrm{T} \sin \theta=\mathrm{W} $$

$$2T\sin\theta = W$$

$$T = \frac{W}{2\sin\theta}$$

Using the trigonometric identity $\frac{1}{\sin\theta} = \cos ec\theta$,

$$T = \frac{W}{2}\cos ec\theta$$

$$\Rightarrow x\cos ec\theta = \frac{W}{2}\cos ec\theta \Rightarrow x = \frac{W}{2}$$

The total weight of the chain is $W = 15\ \text{N}$:

$$x = \frac{15}{2} = 7.5$$

Therefore, the value of $10x$ is $75$.

en.content: A spring scale indicates 10N in the given situation as shown in figure. Neglecting the mass of the pulley and ignoring friction between the cable and pulley, the mass m is:
en.explanation:
When a single inextensible cable passes over ideal pulleys which are massless and frictionless, the tension must be uniform at every point along its length.

The spring scale is connected in series with this cable and indicates a reading of 10 N . Therefore, the constant tension T throughout every single segment of the cable is:

$$ \mathrm{T}_1=10 \mathrm{~N} $$

Since the pulley is massless, the net force acting on it must be zero.

For pulley $2, \mathrm{~T}_1+\mathrm{T}_1=2 \mathrm{~T}_1$ must be balanced by an equal downward force $\mathrm{T}_2$

$$ \mathrm{T}_2=2 \mathrm{~T}_1 $$

For the platform to be at equilibrium,

$$\Sigma F_y = 0 \rightarrow T_1 + T_2 + T_1 = mg$$

$$\Rightarrow T_1 + 2T_1 + T_1 = mg$$

$$\Rightarrow 4T_1 = mg \Rightarrow 4 \times 10 = m \times 10$$

$$\Rightarrow 40 = 10 \cdot m \Rightarrow m = \frac{40}{10} = 4\,\text{kg}$$

Therefore, the mass of the platform is $4\,\text{kg}$.

en.content: A weight $W$ is supported by two cables as shown. The tension in the cable making angle $\theta$ with horizontal will be the minimum when the value of $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ is :
en.explanation:
The string with tension $\mathrm{T}_1$ is at an angle of $60^{\circ}$ above the horizontal.

The string with tension $\mathrm{T}_2$ is inclined at an angle $\theta$ above the horizontal.

The weight W acts vertically downward.

For the knot to remain at rest, the vector sum of all forces along both the horizontal and vertical axes must equal zero.

Along the horizontal axis,

$$\Sigma F_x = 0 \Rightarrow T_1 \cos(60^\circ) = T_2 \cos \theta$$

$$T_1 = \frac{T_2 \cos \theta}{\cos(60^\circ)} \Rightarrow T_1 = 2T_2 \cos \theta \ldots (i)$$

Along the vertical axis,

$$\Sigma F_y = 0 \Rightarrow T_1 \sin(60^\circ) + T_2 \sin \theta = W \ldots (ii)$$

On substituting expression for $T_1$ from equation (i) into equation (i) :

$$(2T_2 \cos \theta) \sin(60^\circ) + T_2 \sin \theta = W$$

$$T_2 [2 \cos \theta \sin(60^\circ) + \sin \theta] = W$$

$$T_2\left[2\cos\theta\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)+\sin\theta\right]=W$$

$$T_2\left(\sqrt{3}\cos\theta+\sin\theta\right)=W$$

On multiplying and dividing left-hand side by $\sqrt{(\sqrt{3})^2+(1)^2}=\sqrt{3+1}=\sqrt{4}=2$:

$$2T_2\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\cos\theta+\frac{1}{2}\sin\theta\right)=W$$

$$2T_2\left(\sin(60^\circ)\cos\theta+\cos(60^\circ)\sin\theta\right)=W$$

$$2T_2\sin(60^\circ+\theta)=W$$

$$T_2=\frac{W}{2\sin(60^\circ+\theta)}$$

To make the tension $T_2$ as small as possible, the denominator of must be maximized. The maximum possible value that a sine function is $1$, which occurs when angle is $90^\circ$:

$$\sin(60^\circ+\theta)=1 \Rightarrow 60^\circ+\theta=90^\circ$$

$$\theta=90^\circ-60^\circ=30^\circ$$

Therefore, the value of $\theta$ is $30^\circ$.
